title: The Word That Means Pulled Apart
subtitle: On what these verses are actually asking, and what they have wrongly been used to demand
teaser: The verb in “be anxious for nothing” is the same verb Paul uses two chapters earlier as a compliment, and the same one Jesus says gently to Martha by name. Whatever these verses forbid, it is not caring — and it was never handed to you as a rebuke.
theme: The command is not to stop feeling but to redirect the load, and the misuse of these verses against anxious people collapses on the Greek.
framework: Matthew 6:25-30; Philippians 4:6 — be careful for nothing

modules.passage: Therefore I say unto you, Be not anxious for your life, what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink; nor yet for your body, what ye shall put on. Is not the life more than the food, and the body than the raiment? Behold the birds of the heaven, that they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; and your heavenly Father feedeth them. Are not ye of much more value than they?
modules.scriptureContext: Two minutes with a verse that has been used, more than once, as a stick.

modules.definition: to be anxious, to worry — and also, in the same lexicons, to care for, to look out for, to be concerned about something
modules.usage: This is the verb in “be not anxious” and in “be anxious for nothing.” It appears nineteen times in the New Testament, and the range is wider than the English suggests: Thayer's gives both “to be troubled with cares” and “to care for, look out for a thing.” One word covers the fear and the caring.

modules.heading: Before Anything Else, One Thing Said Plainly
modules.content:
These verses get used as a weapon, and that has to be said out loud before anything else can be said honestly.

“Be not anxious.” “Be anxious for nothing.” People carrying real fear — about money, about a diagnosis, about a child — have been handed those lines as a rebuke, with the clear implication that a better Christian would not feel this. Some have been told their anxiety is a sin to repent of. Some have been told it is evidence of weak faith.

That use of these verses does not survive contact with the verses themselves, and the rest of this week will show why in detail.

Here is the short version. The same verb Paul uses in “be anxious for nothing” he uses two chapters earlier as a compliment. He says Timothy will genuinely care — the same word — for the Philippians' welfare. He uses it again for how members of a church should look out for one another.

A word Paul praises in one letter is not a word he criminalises in the next.

So whatever these verses are doing, they are not shaming you for caring, and they are not a command to stop feeling things. Today is about finding out what they are actually doing, which turns out to be gentler and considerably more practical.

modules.prompt: Has one of these verses ever been used on you — or by you — as a rebuke? What did it produce?

modules.heading: A Two-Minute Prayer
modules.prayerText: Lord, I have been told to stop feeling this, and trying has only added shame to the fear. Let me hear what You are actually saying today. Amen.

modules.ctaSubtext: That can be the whole of today. Below, when there is time: the same verb used as a compliment, a word that cannot decide between height and time and teaches something either way, and bread in the desert that went bad on purpose if anyone kept it overnight.

modules.passage: Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.
modules.scriptureContext: The King James “careful” is the older sense — full of care, weighed down by it. The modern word has drifted a long way from what Paul wrote.

modules.heading: The Verb Paul Uses As A Compliment
modules.content:
Nineteen times in the New Testament, and the pattern in those nineteen is the argument.

In Philippians 2:20, Paul is explaining why he is sending Timothy rather than someone else. He says he has no one else like him, who will genuinely care for their welfare. The verb is merimnaō. It is offered as the reason Timothy is worth sending.

In 1 Corinthians 12:25, Paul describes how a body of believers should work — that there should be no division, but that the members should have the same care one for another. The same verb again, this time as an instruction about how a church ought to function.

So the vocabulary is settled before we reach Philippians 4. Paul has already used this word for something he wants more of.

And then there is Luke 10:41, which is the one that should end the argument. Martha is working while her sister sits, and she complains about it, and Jesus answers her. Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things.

That is merimnaō. Said to her face, using her name, twice — which in that idiom is tenderness rather than reprimand. He is not telling her she has sinned. He is telling her, gently, that she is being pulled in too many directions at once, and that there is something better available to her right now.

One lexicon glosses the word as being drawn in opposite directions, divided into parts, pulled apart. That reading is a lexicon's, not a bare fact of the etymology, and it is worth stating carefully. But it fits what the passages actually describe: not a person feeling too much, but a person being pulled toward too many things at once with no centre holding.

Which is a very different diagnosis, and it calls for a different response. You do not fix being pulled apart by trying harder not to feel pulled. You fix it, if it can be fixed, by something at the centre strong enough to hold the pieces together.

modules.definition: stature — and also age, time of life, the span of a life. Thayer's glosses it as maturity, in years or in size.
modules.usage: This single word is why the translations split in Matthew 6:27. The King James reads “add one cubit unto his stature,” treating it as height. Most modern versions read “add a single hour to his life,” treating it as time. The American Standard splits the difference with “one cubit unto the measure of his life.”
modules.usageNote: Neither side is wrong. The Greek genuinely carries both, and the verse does not disambiguate. It is one of the places where honest translators reach different defensible answers, and it is more useful to see the seam than to have it smoothed over.

relatedWords.reference: Used of Zacchaeus being short of stature — unambiguously physical height.

Used of Sarah being past the age of childbearing — unambiguously time. Eight New Testament occurrences in all, and the range runs across both senses, which is why Matthew 6:27 cannot be settled by the word alone.

modules.content: Whether the verse means you cannot add an inch or cannot add an hour, the point survives: worry has never once succeeded at the job it claims to be doing.

modules.passage: And which of you by being anxious can add one cubit unto the measure of his life? And why are ye anxious concerning raiment? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin: yet I say unto you, that even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. But if God doth so clothe the grass of the field, which to-day is, and to-morrow is cast into the oven, shall he not much more clothe you, O ye of little faith?
modules.scriptureContext: An argument from results. Not “stop feeling that,” but “notice what it has produced.”
redLetter: And which of you by being anxious can add one cubit unto the measure of his life? And why are ye anxious concerning raiment? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin: yet I say unto you, that even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. But if God doth so clothe the grass of the field, which to-day is, and to-morrow is cast into the oven, shall he not much more clothe you, O ye of little faith?

modules.heading: An Argument, Not An Order
modules.content:
Look at the form of what Jesus is doing here, because the form is the pastoral care.

He does not say worry is wicked. He does not tell them to repent of it. He asks a question about outcomes: which of you, by being anxious, can add one cubit — or one hour — to your life?

It is an appeal to their own experience. You have done this. You have lain awake and run the numbers. Did it lengthen anything? Did the account change while you were doing it?

Everyone honest knows the answer, and it lands without shame because it is not an accusation. It is an observation about a tool that does not work.

Then He points at birds and flowers, which is not sentimental. He is arguing from the lesser to the greater, a standard form: if God dresses grass that will be fuel by the weekend, the case for you is stronger, not weaker.

And then a phrase that is easy to hear as a slap. O ye of little faith.

But notice where it sits. It is the conclusion of the encouragement, not the opening of a rebuke. He has just spent three verses building the case that they are more valuable than birds and better dressed than Solomon. The phrase lands on people He is in the middle of reassuring. It is closer to “why do you not believe how safe you are” than to “how dare you be afraid.”

The difference between those two readings is the difference between a verse that helps an anxious person and a verse that flattens them.

modules.heading: He Did Not Abolish The Work
modules.content:
Chrysostom saw the obvious objection coming and closed it in the next homily.

If the birds do not sow and the lilies do not spin, is this a sermon against working for a living?

His answer is exact.

"In fact, the labor lies, not in taking no thought, but in taking thought for these things."

Then he applies it to each image in turn. Of the birds, he says it "was not the sowing that He did away with, but the anxious thought."

Of the lilies: He "put an end not to the work, but to the care."

The work stays. The exhausting part was never the work.
modules.historicalContext: Homily XXII on the Gospel of St. Matthew, on Matthew 6:28-29, in the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers translation (Prevost/Riddle, 1888).

modules.heading: Where This Day Sits in the Story
modules.ancientTruth: The crowd hearing this lived without savings, insurance, or reliable storage. A day labourer was hired in the morning and paid at dusk, and a day without work was a day without food. When Jesus talks about what to eat tomorrow, He is speaking to people for whom that was a live question every day of their lives.
modules.modernApplication: The mechanism has changed and the arithmetic has not. Most people still have a point past which the money does not reach, and most people still find it at three in the morning.
modules.connectionPoint: Yesterday established the order — seek first, and the adding is God's work. Today takes up what happens in a person while they wait to see whether that is true, and refuses to call that reaction a sin.
modules.newTestamentEcho: Peter picks up the noun form of this word and gives it a direction rather than a prohibition: “Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.” The care does not evaporate. It gets moved.

modules.passage: Then Moses said to them, “No one may keep any of it until morning.” But they did not listen to Moses; some people left part of it until morning, and it became infested with maggots and began to smell. So Moses was angry with them. Every morning each one gathered as much as was needed, and when the sun grew hot, it melted away.
emphasis: No one may keep any of it until morning
modules.scriptureContext: God's own food supply, engineered so that it could not be stockpiled.

modules.heading: Bread That Would Not Keep
modules.content:
There is an Old Testament passage sitting underneath this whole sermon, and it explains the strange shape of the instruction.

In the wilderness, God feeds Israel with manna. The arrangement has a rule attached: gather what you need for today, and keep none of it overnight. Some of them try anyway. What they kept bred worms and stank by morning.

Read that as a piece of design rather than a punishment. God supplied food that could not be hoarded. The spoilage was not a malfunction; it was the point. Deuteronomy says as much when it looks back on the period — that He humbled them and let them hunger and fed them with manna, so that they would learn that people do not live by bread alone.

Forty years of that. Not a lesson taught once, but a daily arrangement, every morning, for a generation.

And four verses before “seek ye first,” in the same sermon, Jesus teaches them to pray for exactly this. Give us this day our daily bread. One day's worth. The same economy, now in a prayer.

So the thing being asked of the anxious person is not a feeling. It is a practice, and it is the oldest one in the book: take today's provision, do not try to secure the year, and come back tomorrow.

That is genuinely difficult, and it is difficult in a specific way worth naming. It is difficult because it does not permit the thing anxiety most wants, which is to be finished. Anxiety wants a settlement — one arrangement solid enough that the question never has to be asked again. The manna arrangement never offered that to anybody. It offered enough, and then it offered enough again.

Which means the person waking up afraid again on Wednesday, having trusted on Tuesday, is not failing at this. They are inside the arrangement as designed.

modules.videoTitle: The Lord’s Prayer Could Rewire Your Daily Life
modules.videoCaption: On the prayer that sits four verses before this promise, including the line that asks for one day's bread and no more.

modules.heading: What He Was Actually Afraid Of
modules.content:
John Bunyan was arrested in November 1660 for preaching without a licence and held in the county jail at Bedford. He was there, by his own count, for twelve years.

He had two strategies for surviving it, and he wrote both down. He would pass, as he put it, a sentence of death upon every thing that can properly be called a thing of this life. And he would count the grave his house.

Then he admits, in writing, that the strategies did not work.

"But notwithstanding these helps, I found myself a man and compassed with infirmities." Parting from his wife and children had often been to him in that place, he says, "as the pulling the flesh from the bones." And then he names the specific one. "Especially my poor blind child, who lay nearer my heart than all besides."

What he feared for her was not abstract. He spells it out: "Poor child! thought I, what sorrow art thou like to have for thy portion in this world! Thou must be beaten, must beg, suffer hunger, cold, nakedness, and a thousand calamities, though I cannot now endure the wind should blow upon thee."

There is no resolution in the passage. The nearest thing to one is a sentence that concedes everything: "I must venture you all with God, though it goeth to the quick to leave you."
modules.connectionToTheme: This is what merimnaō looks like from the inside, written by a man nobody would accuse of weak faith. He is not anxious about a mood. He is anxious about whether a blind child will be beaten and go hungry. And Scripture's own answer, which he reaches, is not that the fear was wrong — it is that the child had to be ventured with God, and that doing so went to the quick.

modules.heading: What Paul Actually Instructs
modules.content:
Come back now to the verse that gets used as a stick, and read the whole sentence rather than the first three words.

“Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.”

There is a “but” in the middle, and everything after it is the instruction. Paul is not issuing a prohibition and walking away. He is redirecting traffic.

And look at the scope: in every thing. Not in the appropriately spiritual things. Not once you have calmed down enough to pray properly. Every thing — which explicitly includes whatever it is you were anxious about thirty seconds ago.

The word for requests is an ordinary one. It means the things you are asking for. Paul is telling frightened people to say what they want, out loud, to God, specifically and in detail.

So the command is not “feel differently.” It is “take it somewhere.” The instruction assumes the anxiety exists, assumes it will keep arriving, and gives it an address.

This is why the shaming use of the verse is not merely unkind but backwards. It tells a person to stop having the raw material that Paul says to bring. Nobody has ever prayed themselves calm by first pretending they were not afraid.

Peter says the same thing with the same word, in the plainest form it takes anywhere: casting all your care upon him, for he careth for you. Two uses of the same root in one line. Your care goes to Him because He cares about you. It is not a transaction and it is not a technique. It is a reason.

modules.prompt: Paul says to bring your requests “in every thing.” What is the specific, embarrassing, non-spiritual thing you have not actually said to God in words?
additionalQuestions: Where have you been trying to feel differently instead of taking it somewhere?
The manna could not be stored. What are you currently trying to store so that you never have to ask again?

modules.heading: A Practice for Today
modules.instruction: Ten minutes and something to write on. This is Paul's instruction taken literally rather than admired.

steps.title: List them
steps.description: Write down every specific thing you are currently anxious about. Not categories — the actual items, with names and numbers where they have them. Do not tidy the list or rank it.

steps.title: Read it back as a request
steps.description: Go down the list and turn each item into a sentence beginning “I am asking You for.” Say them out loud if you are somewhere you can. This is the “let your requests be made known” step, done in the ordinary sense of the words.

steps.title: Add the thanksgiving
steps.description: Paul includes it in the same sentence, so include it. At the bottom, write one thing that is currently true and good. It does not have to balance the list. It only has to be true.

steps.title: Keep the page
steps.description: Do not throw it away. On Saturday this week's reading comes back to it.

modules.heading: You Are Allowed To Still Be Afraid Tonight
modules.content:
One last thing, because it is the thing most likely to be needed.

Nothing today promised that doing this correctly makes the fear stop. Paul does not say the anxiety will lift. He says the peace of God will guard your heart — which is Friday's subject, and which describes something posted around you, not something that removes the siege.

So if you pray tonight exactly as instructed and wake at three in the morning with the same weight on your chest, you have not failed the exercise.

The manna came every morning for forty years because it was needed every morning for forty years. The arrangement was never that Israel would learn the lesson once and stop being hungry.

And tomorrow this week goes to the hardest place of all — the stretch where a person has done all of this, faithfully, and heard nothing back at all.

For today it is enough to have the verse back the right way round. It was never handed to you as a rebuke. It was handed to you as an address.

modules.heading: What Worry Actually Empties
modules.content:
Alexander Maclaren preached a sermon on these exact verses in Manchester in 1859, and he made a distinction worth keeping.

"Foresight and foreboding are two very different things. It is not that the one is the exaggeration of the other, but the one is opposed to the other."

Then he says what the foreboding costs.

"And what does your anxiety do? It does not empty to-morrow, brother, of its sorrows; but, ah! it empties to-day of its strength. It does not make you escape the evil, it makes you unfit to cope with it when it comes. It does not bless to-morrow, and it robs to-day."

And one more, which is the pastoral heart of it.

"God gives us power to bear all the sorrows of His making; but He does not give us power to bear the sorrows of our own making, which the anticipation of sorrow most assuredly is."
modules.historicalContext: Sermon XVIII, "Anxious Care," on Matthew 6:24-25, in Sermons Preached in Manchester, First Series, pp. 247-248; first published 1859. Worth knowing: the line most people carry on this subject — that worry is like a rocking chair, giving you something to do but getting you nowhere — is not Corrie ten Boom's and not Erma Bombeck's, though it is constantly given to both. It first appears in print in a Delaware newspaper in March 1948, in an unsigned humour column, a year before Bombeck could have written it and six years before ten Boom published in English. Maclaren is the real thing, and he is better.

modules.heading: Prayer
modules.prayerText: Father, I have been ashamed of being afraid, and the shame has been heavier than the fear. You never asked me for the feeling. You asked me for the request. So here it is, in every thing, including the parts I would rather not say in a prayer. I am not going to pretend I am calm. I am going to tell You what I want, and I am going to thank You for what is true, and I am going to do it again tomorrow morning because that is apparently how this works. Amen.
modules.breathPrayer: In: I am not asked to stop feeling — Out: I am asked to bring it

modules.heading: Today's Commitment
modules.commitment: I will stop treating my anxiety as a verdict on my faith, and I will say one specific request out loud to God in plain words.
leavingAtCross: The verse used as a rebuke, by others and by me
The belief that a real Christian would not feel this
The attempt to store up enough that I never have to ask again
receivingFromCross: A verb that Paul uses as a compliment
An instruction with a “but” in the middle of it
Permission to come back tomorrow morning and ask again

modules.heading: One Question
modules.question: Why does the use of “be anxious for nothing” as a rebuke fail on the Greek?
options: Because Paul was writing to a specific church and not to us
Because the same verb is used approvingly elsewhere by Paul — of Timothy caring for the Philippians, and of church members caring for one another
Because the verse is poorly translated in every English version
Because Paul himself was never anxious
modules.explanation: Merimnaō appears nineteen times. Paul uses it as a compliment in Philippians 2:20 and as an instruction to the church in 1 Corinthians 12:25, and Jesus says it gently to Martha by name in Luke 10:41. A word used approvingly in those places is not a word that criminalises caring in Philippians 4:6. Whatever the verse forbids, it is not feeling.

modules.heading: The Voice Behind Today
modules.name: Martha of Bethany
modules.era: first century, a village about two miles from Jerusalem
modules.bio: Host, sister of Mary and Lazarus, and the person to whom Jesus said the word this reading is built on. She appears three times in the Gospels and is working in two of them. She is also the one who, at her brother's tomb, makes one of the clearest confessions of faith anyone makes in John's Gospel.
modules.keyQuote: Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things.
modules.lessonForUs: Martha matters here because of how she is spoken to. Her name is said twice, which is tenderness in that idiom, and the diagnosis is being pulled in many directions rather than sinning. She is not sent away or corrected in front of the room. She is told there is something better available to her in that moment.

relatedScriptures.text: Paul's compliment to Timothy, using the same verb as “be anxious for nothing.” The single most important cross-reference in today's reading.
The same verb again, as an instruction for how members of a church should care for one another.
Martha, named twice, told she is pulled in many directions — the gentlest use of this word in the New Testament.
“Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.” The noun form, redirected rather than forbidden.
God's own explanation, forty years later, of why the manna arrangement worked the way it did.

resources.title: Greek: merimnaō, Strong's G3309
resources.description: Verified at BibleHub. Thayer's gives both “to be anxious; to be troubled with cares” and “to care for, look out for a thing.” Nineteen New Testament occurrences, including Philippians 2:20 and 1 Corinthians 12:25. The “pulled apart” reading quoted in today's teaching is HELPS Word-studies' gloss and is attributed as such rather than treated as plain etymology.

resources.description: Verified at BibleHub. Thayer's carries both “age, time of life” and “stature,” glossed as maturity in years or size — which is why the translations split at Matthew 6:27 and why this reading shows the seam rather than picking a side.

resources.title: Scripture texts
resources.description: Matthew quoted from the American Standard Version, chosen for this day because it renders the verb as “be not anxious,” which sits directly beside the word study. Philippians and 1 Peter from the King James, Exodus and Deuteronomy from the Berean Standard Bible.
